card.definition: An adjective is a word that tells about a noun. It tells what kind, how many, or which one.

example.text: The fluffy kitten slept in the basket.
example.note: Fluffy is the adjective. Kitten is the noun it tells about.

card.how: Fluffy tells what kind of kitten it is.

card.definition: Names of people and names of days and months start with a big letter. A big letter is called a capital letter.

example.text: My friend sam was born on july 3.
example.note: The words that need big letters are Sam and July. The correct sentence is

then.text: My friend Sam was born on July 3.

card.definition: When you list three or more things, put a comma between them. A comma is a small mark that tells the reader to pause.

example.text: I packed a sandwich an apple and a cookie.

then.text: I packed a sandwich, an apple, and a cookie.
then.note: The commas split the list into parts.

card.how: The commas go between the things in the list, so each thing stands on its own.

tips.text: We saw a lion a tiger and a bear.
tips.note: The list is a lion, a tiger, and a bear.

card.definition: Sometimes a sentence starts with a short phrase that tells when or where. Put a comma after that phrase.

example.text: In the morning we eat breakfast.

then.text: In the morning, we eat breakfast.
then.note: The comma comes after the starting phrase.

card.how: The comma gives a small pause after the phrase that tells when.

tips.text: On Monday we go to the park.

card.definition: "Your" means it belongs to you. "You're" is a short way to say "you are." The mark in "you're" takes the place of the letter a.

example.note: Your tells us the lunch box belongs to you.

card.definition: A noun is a word that names a person, a place, or a thing. A common noun names any person, place, or thing, not one special one.

example.text: The dog ran to the park.
example.note: Dog is a noun. It names a thing. Park is a noun. It names a place.

card.how: Ask, "Does this word name a person, a place, or a thing?" If yes, it is a noun.

card.definition: A verb is a word that tells what someone or something does. An action verb shows an action you can do.

example.text: The cat jumps over the fence.
example.note: Jumps is the verb. It tells what the cat does.

card.how: Ask, "What does it do?" The word that answers is the action verb.

using-simple-tenses.title: Using Action Verbs in Simple Tenses

card.definition: Verbs change to show when an action happens. "Today" means it happens now. "Yesterday" means it already happened. "Tomorrow" means it will happen later.

example.text: Today Sam walks to school. Yesterday Sam walked to school. Tomorrow Sam will walk to school.
example.note: Walks is now. Walked is past. Will walk is later.

card.how: The word that tells when, like today or yesterday, helps you pick the right verb form.

tips.text: Today Ana sings. Yesterday Ana sang.
Today Leo plays. Tomorrow Leo will play.

items.text: Today, the dog ___ in the yard.
items.right: Today, the dog plays in the yard.
items.hint: Today means now, so use the present form.

items.right: Yesterday, Ana drew a picture.
items.hint: Yesterday means it already happened, so use the past form.

items.right: Tomorrow, Leo will fly a kite.
items.hint: Tomorrow means it will happen later, so use will plus the verb.

items.hint: Today means now, so use the present form.

items.hint: Tomorrow means it will happen later, so use will plus the verb.
